Silence"}],"\n",["$","blockquote","blockquote-0",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":[["$","em","em-0",{"children":"\"The history of the Caribbean is not only the history of great men and great battles. It is equally the history of the unnamed — those whose labor sustained empires, whose endurance outlasted slavery, and whose descendants still walk the coral soil of these islands.\""}],"\n— Caribbean historian, paraphrasing the broader scholarly consensus on subaltern history in the Anglophone Caribbean"]}],"\n"]}],"\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":[["$","strong","strong-0",{"children":"Alice Deazle"}]," belongs to that vast and largely uncharted archive of Caribbean historical figures whose lives unfolded at the crossroads of slavery, emancipation, and the long, difficult dawn of freedom — yet whose individual stories have been filtered through the coarse mesh of colonial record-keeping, which captured names only incidentally and lives hardly at all. The Deazle family name is rooted in ",["$","strong","strong-1",{"children":"Barbuda"}],", the smaller, often-overlooked sister island of the nation now known as ",["$","strong","strong-2",{"children":"Antigua and Barbuda"}],", and genealogical evidence traces the name as far back as the mid-19th century in that community [7]. It is within this context — Barbuda's singular social history, its unique plantation structure, and its people's remarkable traditions of communal resilience — that Alice Deazle must be understood."]}],"\n",["$","hr","hr-0",{}],"\n",["$","h3","h3-1",{"children":"The Island That Slavery Built Differently"}],"\n",["$","p","p-1",{"children":["To understand any Barbudan woman of the 19th century is to first understand that Barbuda was unlike virtually every other slave island in the British Caribbean. While neighboring ","$L9"," operated as a classic sugar colony — its land scarred by cane fields, its population brutalized by the demands of export agriculture — Barbuda's economy was structured around ","$La"," rather than sugar [1][4]."]}],"\n","$Lb","\n","$Lc","\n","$Ld","\n","$Le","\n","$Lf","\n","$L10","\n","$L11","\n","$L12","\n","$L13","\n","$L14","\n","$L15","\n","$L16","\n","$L17","\n","$L18","\n","$L19","\n","$L1a","\n","$L1b","\n","$L1c","\n","$L1d","\n","$L1e","\n","$L1f","\n","$L20","\n","$L21"]}]]}],"$L22","$L23",false]}],"$L24"]}]

a:["$","strong","strong-1",{"children":"livestock, provisions, and natural resources"}]
b:["$","p","p-2",{"children":["From the late 17th century through emancipation in 1834, Barbuda was leased to the ",["$","strong","strong-0",{"children":"Codrington family"}],", powerful Antiguan planters who used the island primarily as a supply depot: a place to raise cattle, sheep, and provisions to sustain their far more profitable sugar estates on Antigua [2][3]. This meant that Barbuda's enslaved population lived under conditions that differed markedly — though by no means benignly — from those on sugar islands. The enslaved community of Barbuda numbered approximately ",["$","strong","strong-1",{"children":"172 in 1746"}],", growing to over ",["$","strong","strong-2",{"children":"500 by 1831"}]," through natural increase rather than constant importation — a fact remarkable in a region where the mortality rate on sugar estates was so high that constant slave-trading was necessary to maintain plantation workforces [2][3]."]}]
c:["$","p","p-3",{"children":["This demographic stability had profound consequences. Barbudan enslaved people developed ",["$","strong","strong-0",{"children":"deep kinship networks, cultural continuities, and community bonds"}]," over multiple generations. They cultivated their own grounds, fished their own waters, and built a society in the interstices of colonial control [2][4]. Women were central to this society — not merely as reproductive laborers valued for producing the \"natural increase\" that Codrington estate records celebrated, but as the organizers of domestic and community life, the keepers of oral tradition, and the primary providers of nutrition and care [5][6]."]}]
d:["$","hr","hr-1",{}]
e:["$","h3","h3-2",{"children":"Alice Deazle: Life in the Era of Emancipation"}]
f:["$","p","p-4",{"children":["Alice Deazle is believed to have lived during the crucial transition period bracketed by ",["$","strong","strong-0",{"children":"Emancipation (1834)"}]," and the years following ",["$","strong","strong-1",{"children":"full freedom (1838)"}],", when the iniquitous system of \"Apprenticeship\" — which required formerly enslaved people to continue working for their former enslavers for up to six years — finally ended. Based on genealogical records associating the Deazle surname with Barbuda in the mid-19th century [7], Alice's life would have straddled these transformative decades — she may have been born into slavery, or born in the fragile freedom of Apprenticeship, or been a young child when full freedom arrived in 1838."]}]
10:["$","p","p-5",{"children":["For Barbudan women of this era, freedom was not an abstraction — it was a daily negotiation. The Codrington estate retained enormous economic and political power on the island well after emancipation. The Codrington family continued to hold the lease to Barbuda until the British colonial government assumed direct control in ",["$","strong","strong-0",{"children":"1870"}]," [1]. During the Apprenticeship period and beyond, women like Alice navigated a landscape where legal freedom had been declared but economic independence remained elusive. They raised children, maintained the provision grounds that were the community's primary food source, and sustained the intricate social fabric that had allowed Barbudan society to reproduce itself across generations of bondage [2][5]."]}]
11:["$","p","p-6",{"children":["The ",["$","strong","strong-0",{"children":"Deazle name itself"}]," — sometimes rendered in 19th-century records as \"Dizzel\" — appears in Barbudan community history as a family that persisted on the island across generations, suggesting deep roots in the land and community [7]. This kind of multi-generational attachment to place is itself a form of resistance and testimony: in a Caribbean world where enslaved people were routinely displaced, sold, and dispersed, the persistence of a family name on a specific island across more than a century speaks to continuity, community, and the stubborn assertion of belonging."]}]
12:["$","hr","hr-2",{}]
13:["$","h3","h3-3",{"children":"Women's Labour and Community Leadership in Post-Emancipation Barbuda"}]
14:["$","p","p-7",{"children":["In post-emancipation Barbuda, women occupied essential roles that colonial records systematically failed to document. Scholars researching the Codrington estates through the ",["$","strong","strong-0",{"children":"Codrington Renewal and Reconciliation Project"}]," have worked to recover the identities and relationships of Barbudan women, finding in baptismal registers, estate inventories, and census fragments the outlines of lives that official history rendered invisible [7][12]."]}]
15:["$","p","p-8",{"children":"Women like Alice Deazle would have been responsible for:"}]
16:["$","ul","ul-0",{"children":["\n",["$","li","li-0",{"children":[["$","strong","strong-0",{"children":"Provision cultivation:"}]," The kitchen gardens and provision grounds that Barbudan families maintained were women's domains, providing the dietary foundation for community survival [6][8]."]}],"\n",["$","li","li-1",{"children":[["$","strong","strong-0",{"children":"Animal husbandry:"}]," Barbuda's economy centered on livestock, and women participated in the care of these animals, particularly smaller stock such as goats and chickens that were crucial to household food security [5]."]}],"\n",["$","li","li-2",{"children":[["$","strong","strong-0",{"children":"Knowledge transmission:"}]," As the primary caregivers and community educators, Barbudan women of this era were the transmitters of language, spiritual practice, medicinal knowledge, and oral history — the living archive of a people whose written records were held by others [2][4]."]}],"\n",["$","li","li-3",{"children":[["$","strong","strong-0",{"children":"Community governance:"}]," In the years following emancipation, Barbudan communities developed increasingly self-governing social structures, and women — through church networks, extended kinship systems, and community councils — played significant roles in mediating disputes, organizing collective labor, and maintaining social cohesion [4][19]."]}],"\n"]}]
17:["$","p","p-9",{"children":"Barbuda's communal land tradition — which would endure well into the 21st century — has its roots precisely in this period. The island's refusal to allow private land ownership, its insistence on communal access to the island's resources, was shaped by generations of collective survival in which women like Alice Deazle were indispensable participants [4][19]."}]
18:["$","hr","hr-3",{}]
19:["$","h3","h3-4",{"children":"The Silence of the Archive and Its Meaning"}]
1a:["$","p","p-10",{"children":["It must be acknowledged with scholarly honesty that ",["$","strong","strong-0",{"children":"Alice Deazle does not appear in major published Caribbean historical records"}]," as a named, individually documented historical figure. This absence is itself historically significant. The same colonial archive that meticulously recorded sugar yields, livestock inventories, and the sale prices of enslaved people routinely failed to preserve the names, achievements, and voices of Caribbean women — especially those of African descent [5][10]."]}]
1b:["$","p","p-11",{"children":["As historian ",["$","strong","strong-0",{"children":"Dr. Natasha Lightfoot"}]," and others working in Antiguan and Barbudan history have documented, the recovery of women's lives in this era requires reading against the grain of colonial records, finding meaning in what is omitted as much as in what is stated [17]. The fact that the Deazle name persists in Barbudan community life across nearly two centuries — from genealogical fragments of the 1820s through contemporary Barbudans who carry the name today [1][2][3] — is itself a form of historical testimony: testimony to survival, to rootedness, and to the tenacious human insistence on being remembered."]}]
1c:["$","p","p-12",{"children":["Alice Deazle, whatever the full particulars of her individual life, represents the tens of thousands of Caribbean women whose labor built islands, whose endurance survived slavery, and whose descendants now carry the weight and the gift of that history. She is, in this sense, not merely one woman — she is the embodied history of ",["$","strong","strong-0",{"children":"Barbudan womanhood in the age of emancipation"}],"."]}]
1d:["$","hr","hr-4",{}]
1e:["$","h3","h3-5",{"children":"Legacy and Recognition"}]
1f:["$","p","p-13",{"children":["The legacy of women like Alice Deazle is carried forward today in the ongoing work of historians, genealogists, and community organizations committed to recovering Caribbean women's history from colonial archives. The ",["$","strong","strong-0",{"children":"Codrington Renewal and Reconciliation Project"}],", in partnership with universities including the University of Birmingham, has worked to map the kinship networks of Barbudan enslaved communities, restoring names and relationships to the historical record [7][12]. This work represents the kind of institutional commitment that can, over time, transform figures like Alice Deazle from shadows into people."]}]
20:["$","p","p-14",{"children":["Barbuda itself stands as a living monument to the communal values and traditions that women like Alice helped sustain — values of collective land stewardship, deep community bonds, and fierce attachment to place that survived slavery, survived colonialism, and in recent times survived the devastation of ",["$","strong","strong-0",{"children":"Hurricane Irma (2017)"}],". When Barbudans fought to return to and rebuild their island after Irma, they drew on precisely the reserves of communal resilience that generations of Barbudan women had spent centuries building [6][3]."]}]
21:["$","p","p-15",{"children":"In honoring Alice Deazle, we honor all of them."}]
22:["$","$L28",null,{"title":"Learn about the legacy of Alice Deazle","url":"https://caribbeanlegacyarchive.com/profiles/alice-deazle"}]
29:T49d,Alice Deazle's contributions, like those of countless Caribbean women of her era, must be understood in terms of collective rather than individual impact. As a member of the Barbudan community during the emancipation era, she and women like her sustained the provision grounds, kinship networks, oral traditions, and communal governance structures that allowed Barbudan society to survive and maintain its distinctive identity through slavery and into freedom. The communal land traditions of Barbuda — which endured for nearly two centuries after emancipation and became internationally recognized as a unique model of collective land stewardship — were maintained in large part by the labor and social organization of women within the community. Beyond the material, women like Alice Deazle served as the living archive of Barbudan culture: transmitting language, spiritual knowledge, medicinal practice, and oral history across generations in the absence of written records. Her legacy is best understood as part of the collective legacy of Barbudan women — a legacy of extraordinary endurance, communal solidarity, and the insistence on belonging to a place and a people.23:["$","div",null,{"className":"mb-12 pt-12 border-t border-gold/10","children":[["$","h2",null,{"className":"font-serif font-bold text-3xl text-navy mb-6","children":"Major Contributions"}],["$","div",null,{"className":"text-navy/80 text-xl leading-relaxed bg-white p-8 border-l-4 border-tropical-green shadow-sm","children":"$29"}]]}]
